title: If you're a Brahmin
hookLine: Kabir asks, if birth made you high, why weren't you born by some other road (Gauri, Kabir, ang 324)

cards: A question can do what an argument can't. Ask someone where they were born, and you learn a city. Ask how they were born, and everyone in the room gives the same answer.
Same way in. Same cry. Same small, wet, helpless start.

A weaver in Kashi once turned that plain fact into a question for a learned man who thought his birth made him higher. The question is still sitting in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Gauri, waiting for whoever reads it.

teach.b: Kabir starts in the womb. In the womb, he says, there's no family line and no caste; everyone comes from the same seed of the Divine.
Then he turns to the pandit, the learned man, and asks: tell me, since when have you been a Brahmin? Don't waste your life just saying the word. Then the question from today's title.

teach.h: WHY NOT BY SOME OTHER ROAD?
teach.b: If you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come into the world by some other road? He presses it with a picture. How are you a Brahmin and I a Shudra?

teach.h: BLOOD IN MINE, MILK IN YOURS?
teach.b: Is it blood in my veins and milk in yours? You can hear the weaver's humor. He isn't shouting.
He's asking a question so plain that pride has nowhere to stand. And Kabir doesn't throw away the word Brahmin. He gives it a new meaning.
The hymn ends: Kabir says, whoever reflects on God, that one we call a Brahmin. So the line isn't against a people or a faith. It's against the idea that birth decides worth.
Sikhs hear this hymn beside the Gurus' own teaching, which also refused to rank people by caste, and beside the langar, where everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food.
Whatever titles come later, every one of us was born the same way.

how: Sikhs sing this Gauri hymn of Kabir in kirtan, and teachers connect it with langar and the Gurus' rejection of caste, where all sit together on the floor and share one meal.

o: in Kabir's hymn, anyone born in Kashi
in Kabir's hymn, whoever reflects on God
in Kabir's hymn, a title to throw away

games.q: if you're a Brahmin — tap the pairs.

games.q: you're Kabir, a weaver. a learned man says his birth makes him higher than you. what do you do?
o: insult his family and his faith.
ask him a plain question about how he was born.
games.why: Kabir asks: if you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come by some other road? then he says whoever reflects on God is the Brahmin.

practice: Bring to mind one person you tend to look up to too much, or down on without noticing, a boss, a cleaner, a celebrity, a cousin, and picture them as Kabir does: arriving in the world the same way you did, small and crying.
Hold that picture for a few breaths, then see them as they are now, and notice if anything has leveled out. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once for them and once for you.

wordCard.voice: Brahmin. Kabir's question to the proud, learned man: if birth made you one, why weren't you born by some other road?

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, as the hymn writes it: a Brahmin. Kabir keeps the word and gives it to whoever reflects on God.

carryVoice: Your line: born the same way. Same small start, and the same worth. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Gauri, Kabir, Ang 324 (no caste in the womb; 'if you are a Brahmin born of a Brahmin mother'; blood and milk; whoever reflects on God)
